section_summary: This section covers the turbulent period in Japanese domestic politics from December 1931 through June 1932, documenting the fall of the Wakatsuki Cabinet and the installation of the Seiyukai government under Prime Minister Tsuyoshi Inukai. It details the February 1932 general elections in which the Seiyukai won a commanding majority, the subsequent assassination of Prime Minister Inukai by young naval and army officers in the May 15 Incident, and the ensuing collapse of party-led cabinets. Diplomatic despatches, telegrams, and State Department memoranda chronicle the formation of a national unity compromise government under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito, assessing its cabinet roster, the dominant influence of War Minister Sadao Araki and military factions, and looming crises involving agrarian unrest, zaibatsu dominance, economic depression, and the recognition of Manchukuo.

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting on the dissolution of the 60th Diet and analyzing party platforms, issues, and prospects for the February 1932 election.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes reports that the 60th Diet was dissolved by Imperial Ordinance on January 21, 1932, and the Inukai Cabinet scheduled general elections for February 20. The Government dissolved the Lower House immediately after opening speeches to preempt the Minseito majority from mounting an attack over the Sakuradamon incident. The despatch contrasts the party platforms: the Seiyukai advocates bond financing, a five-year industrial plan, rice monopolies, suspension of the gold standard, and cooperation with the Army in Manchuria, while the Minseito supports deflation, the gold standard, and tax increases. Forbes predicts a Seiyukai victory due to government control over local election officials, extensive campaign funding from banking profits after the gold embargo, and Inukai's shrewd leadership.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 471: Dissolution of the Diet and the Forthcoming General Elections

subfiles.title: Document File Note: Despatch No. 509 (894.002/178)

subfiles.about: Exhaustive diplomatic despatch analyzing the results, structural causes, and systemic ramifications of the Seiyukai's landslide victory in the 1932 general election.
subfiles.summary: Counselor Neville provides an in-depth analysis of the February 20, 1932 general election, in which the ruling Seiyukai won a historic landslide of 304 seats while the Minseito plummeted to 147. The defeat of the Minseito is attributed to internal fractures following Hamaguchi's death, Adachi's defection, and the assassination of campaign manager Junnosuke Inouye just prior to voting, alongside widespread public rejection of deflationary retrenchment. The Seiyukai benefited decisively from official control over prefectural governors and police, generous campaign funds from financial firms benefiting from the reimposed gold embargo, and public rally-around-the-flag sentiment regarding military actions in China. The report examines the declining influence of proletarian parties, growing popular cynicism toward parliamentarism and fears of fascism, and noteworthy individual contests, including the election of the first Korean Diet member, Boku Shin Kin.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 509: Detailed Report on the Japanese General Election of February 20, 1932

subfiles.about: Ambassador Forbes transmits personal impressions of easing political tensions in Tokyo and encloses an address delivered by Navy Minister Osumi praising Japanese-American naval ties.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Forbes writes confidentially to Secretary Stimson that political tension in Tokyo has eased noticeably, citing reports from European diplomats and journalists. He describes interactions with Japanese military leaders, remarking on the cordiality of War Minister Sadao Araki and Admiral Toyoda compared to the evasiveness of retired General Sato. Forbes encloses the formal address delivered by Minister of the Navy Admiral Mineo Osumi at a farewell luncheon on March 18, 1932. Osumi's speech commends Forbes for easing international misunderstandings surrounding Manchuria and Shanghai and stresses the importance of naval friendship as an anchor of peace.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Forbes to Secretary of State Stimson Transmitting Address by Admiral Mineo Osumi

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch reporting on the formation, personnel, factional balance, public reactions, and challenges of the Saito Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: Chargé Neville provides an extensive examination of the newly installed Cabinet formed under Admiral Viscount Makoto Saito following the assassination of Prime Minister Inukai by young officers. The despatch explains that the administration represents an uneasy compromise between military radicals demanding an end to party politics and Prince Saionji's defense of constitutionalism. Neville provides biographical and political analyses of all twelve ministers, identifying Saito, War Minister Araki, Finance Minister Takahashi, and Home Minister Yamamoto as the only leaders of high caliber, while noting that Araki effectively dominates policy. Public, political, and financial circles are described as disappointed by the ministry's mediocre composition, as it faces unprecedented domestic crises of agrarian distress, debt, and zaibatsu resentment alongside international tensions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 635: The Saito Cabinet
